content.text:
Your sync is failing. The UI just doesn't tell you.

**Why it fails:** GitHub is rejecting the token. Every time you click sync, the container logs show:

```
TransportException: https://<token>@github.com/MadeInShineA/data-viz-project.git:
git-upload-pack not permitted
```

GitHub returns "git-upload-pack not permitted" when a token is valid but isn't allowed to read that repo. You first tried with the `oauth2` username and then with a fine-grained PAT (`github_pat_…`), and both were refused. With a fine-grained PAT this usually means one of two things:

- **Repository access** doesn't include `MadeInShineA/data-viz-project`. The token is limited to "selected repositories" and this repo isn't one of them.
- **Repository permissions → Contents** isn't set to at least **Read-only**. Metadata-only isn't enough to clone or fetch.

**Why it still says "sync worked":** in `CheckpointSyncServiceImpl.syncRepo` (`server/src/main/java/com/mzfuture/entire/checkpoint/service/impl/CheckpointSyncServiceImpl.java:85-91`), listing the remote refs fails, the code logs a WARN and does a plain `return`. The controller then answers with success. Nothing gets written, so the last-sync time stays null ("never synced") and there are no checkpoints.

**What to do:**

1. On GitHub, go to Settings → Developer settings → Fine-grained tokens and edit the token. Add `data-viz-project` under Repository access and set Contents to Read-only. If you'd rather start fresh, create a new token with those settings.
2. Update the token in the dashboard's repo settings and sync again.

**Revoke that PAT.** JGit puts the token in the remote URL, so the full token is printed in plain text in the container logs (`podman logs entire-dashboard`). Anyone who can read those logs can use it, so rotate it rather than just fixing its permissions.

I can also fix the code so that failures like this come back to the UI as an error instead of a fake success, and so the token is removed from logged URLs. Want me to do that?
But when I validate the token inside the ui it says its valid

content.text:
That's expected, because the "validate" button checks something different from what sync needs.

`GithubAdapter.validateToken` (`adapter/GithubAdapter.java:42-63`) only calls `GET https://api.github.com/user` and treats a 200 as "valid." That proves the token exists and hasn't expired. Any fine-grained PAT gets a 200 there, even one with no repository access and no permissions at all. The repo URL isn't even used: `webUrl` is passed in but ignored.

Sync has to clone and fetch `MadeInShineA/data-viz-project`, which needs **Contents: Read** on that specific repo. So the token can pass validation and still be refused by GitHub, which is exactly the "git-upload-pack not permitted" error in your logs.

You can confirm this yourself with the token:

```
! curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://api.github.com/repos/MadeInShineA/data-viz-project/contents
```

A 404 or 403 here, when `/user` returns 200, means the token can't see the repo. A 200 means it can.

**The fix on your side** is the same as before: edit the PAT on GitHub, add `data-viz-project` under Repository access, and set Contents to Read-only. Since the current token is printed in plain text in the container logs, it's safer to create a new one with those settings and revoke the old one.

**On the code side,** there are three things worth fixing, and I can make them if you want:
1. Have validation call `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}` using the repo URL and require `permissions.pull`. A wrong token would then fail at validation instead of at sync.
2. Have `syncRepo` send failures back to the UI as errors instead of returning silently, so the UI stops saying sync worked when it didn't.
3. Remove the token from the URLs written to the logs.
Please make thos changes, also fix that it's actually sayingsuccess even if it doesn't actually success

content.text:
I made all three changes. The code compiles and the tests pass (10 tests, including 4 new ones for the token masking). I haven't tried them in the running app yet. Your container is still the old `ghcr.io/madeinshinea/entire-dashboard:0.1.10` image, so you won't see any difference until you rebuild it, either with a local `podman build` or by publishing a new image tag.

**1. Sync no longer says "success" when it failed**
- `syncRepo` in `CheckpointSyncServiceImpl.java` used to return quietly on every failure, and the server then answered "OK". Now each failure is reported as an error, and the existing error box in the sync window shows the real reason.
- Two new error codes in `Errors.java`:
  - **`GIT_REMOTE_ERROR` (502):** GitHub refused the request, for example because of the token. I avoided 401/403 because the dashboard reads those as "your login expired" and would try to refresh your session.
  - **`NO_CHECKPOINTS` (422):** the repo has neither the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch nor any `refs/entire/checkpoints/` refs. This used to look like a successful sync too.
- A repo with checkpoint data but no other branches still counts as a successful sync with nothing to process, so its "last synced" time gets set.
- The scheduled sync of all repos logs each failing repo and carries on with the others.

**2. Token validation checks access to the repo**
- In `GitSyncServiceImpl.validateToken`, after the existing GitHub login check, it now lists the repo's branches over git, the same way sync does. A token that can log in but can't read the repo fails with "Token is valid but cannot read this repository", plus a hint about Contents: Read-only.
- This works for GitHub, GitLab, Gitea and Gitee, since it uses git itself rather than a GitHub-only API call.

**3. Tokens no longer end up in logs or error messages**
- New `common/util/SecretMasker.java` turns `https://<token>@host` into `https://***@host`, and also hides tokens starting with `github_pat_`, `ghp_` and `glpat-`.
- All git failures in `GitOperationServiceImpl` now go through one helper. It hides the token, logs one line instead of a stack trace (the stack trace contained the token several times), and adds the permission hint when access is refused.
- This also closes a second leak: the old error messages sent to the browser contained the full token URL.

Two more things:
- **Old logs:** the logs of the current container still contain your old token. Revoking that token on GitHub is the real fix.
- **Edit form:** I didn't check whether the repo edit form re-sends the saved token or an empty field when you click "Validate" there.
